glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: David confesses the LORD as his Shepherd, who provides for him, stays with him through the darkest valley, and welcomes him as an honored guest to a lifetime in His house.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: “A Psalm of David” (23:1) stands between Psalm 22, where a cry of abandonment turns to praise, and Psalm 24, where the King of glory enters His holy hill. No occasion is named; the words come from the shepherd who became Israel’s king.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.” (Psalm 23:1, NKJV)

cards.title: Author
cards.html: The title attributes the psalm to David (23:1). He had kept his father’s sheep and defended them from the lion and the bear (1 Samuel 17:34–37) before God took him “from the sheepfolds” to shepherd Israel (Psalm 78:70–72). The psalm most likely voices the settled trust of a man looking back over a long life under the LORD’s care.

cards.title: Occasion
cards.html: The psalm names no occasion. Events in David’s life give its lines color, such as Saul’s pursuit and the provisions brought to him in the wilderness during Absalom’s revolt (2 Samuel 17:29), but none of them is its stated setting. David wrote it in the first person, and it became the prayer of every worshiper who makes the same confession.

cards.title: Psalm Type
cards.html: A psalm of trust. It uses two pictures of the same LORD: the shepherd who leads and protects (23:1–4) and the host who welcomes and honors (23:5–6). At verse 4, in the darkest part of the journey, David stops speaking about the LORD and begins speaking to Him.

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Psalm 23 begins with its whole message in one line: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (23:1). Kings in the ancient world were called shepherds of their people, and Scripture gives the title to God Himself. Here the shepherd-king David confesses that he is a sheep, and that under this Shepherd he lacks nothing he truly needs. The rest and provision that follow come from His leading: green pastures, still waters, a soul restored, and right paths “for His name’s sake” (23:3).

Then the road goes down into “the valley of the shadow of death” (23:4). The psalm does not pretend the danger is unreal. What changes is the way David speaks. He turns from “He” to “You”: “I will fear no evil; For You are with me.” That line stands at the heart of the psalm. David’s courage rests on the Shepherd’s presence, not on escape, and the rod that defends and the staff that guides are his comfort.

In verse 5 the Shepherd becomes a host. He prepares a table “in the presence of my enemies,” anoints His guest’s head with oil and fills his cup to overflowing. The enemies are still there, but the LORD’s welcome stands in full view of them. And where enemies once hunted David, he now says that goodness and mercy will “follow” him, a word that usually means to pursue (23:6). The psalm ends with the hope of dwelling in the house of the LORD, a whole life lived in God’s presence.

Read through the rest of Scripture, these same pictures open onto the believer’s life with God. The table points to communion with God in the presence of the enemies of the soul, seen most fully at the Lord’s table, “the communion of the blood of Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:16). The rod and staff speak of the Shepherd’s loving discipline and guidance (Hebrews 12:6). The oil points to the Holy Spirit, who came upon David at his anointing (1 Samuel 16:13) and abides in believers (1 John 2:27). Psalm 23 does not name Jesus, but the LORD who shepherded David is the One who says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Psalm 23:1–3 — The LORD Is My Shepherd

David confesses the LORD as his Shepherd and finds in Him everything he needs: rest, refreshment, a revived soul and guidance on right paths. The LORD leads this way for the honor of His own name.

Psalm 23:4 — Through the Valley, You Are with Me

In the darkest valley, where death itself is near, David speaks directly to the LORD and fears no evil because the Shepherd is with him. The rod and staff that protect and guide become his comfort.

Psalm 23:5–6 — The LORD’s Table and the LORD’s House

The LORD welcomes David as His honored guest, setting a table before his enemies, anointing his head and filling his cup. Goodness and mercy pursue him all his days, and his hope is to dwell in the LORD’s house.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Psalm 23 shows a trust that looks danger in the face. It speaks of want, a dark valley and enemies, and it confesses the LORD in the middle of them all. In this psalm, faith rests on the Shepherd who is present inside the threat.

The psalm also belongs to the whole of life, not only to funerals. Its pastures, paths, valley and table cover ordinary days as well as the last one, and its closing hope reaches from “all the days of my life” to dwelling with God. Because the LORD shepherds His people in Christ, every believer can make David’s confession personally: the Shepherd provides, stays near in the dark and welcomes His own home.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The LORD as Shepherd-King. The divine name joined to a royal title makes the LORD David’s own Shepherd (23:1).

Rest and restoration. The Shepherd leads to rest, revives the soul and guides on right paths for His name’s sake (23:2–3).

Presence in the valley. “For You are with me” stands at the center of the psalm (23:4).

Welcome before enemies. The host’s table, oil and full cup honor the guest in full view of his enemies (23:5).

A lifetime of goodness and mercy. God’s goodness and steadfast love pursue David to the end of his days and into the LORD’s house (23:6).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
YHWH-Rohi. From the Hebrew of 23:1, meaning the LORD my Shepherd. It is a confession drawn from this line rather than a separate name used elsewhere in Scripture.

“Restores my soul.” The Hebrew word for soul means the whole living person. The phrase describes the reviving of a weary or failing life (23:3).

“The shadow of death.” The NKJV’s rendering in 23:4. Many scholars read the Hebrew as a single word for deep darkness; either way, the valley is a place of mortal danger.

Rod and staff. The rod was a club for defense and could stand for authority; the staff was a support for walking and guiding (23:4). Scripture links the rod with God’s oversight of His flock (Ezekiel 20:37).

“You anoint my head.” The verb here describes the refreshing oil a host gave an honored guest, not the word used for anointing kings and priests (23:5).

Goodness and mercy. Goodness translates the Hebrew word tov; mercy translates hesed, God’s steadfast, faithful love. The verb “follow” usually means to pursue, so these blessings chase David down for life (23:6).

items.title: God’s Leading: To Rest and On the Right Path
items.html: “He leads me” appears twice in these verses, with two different Hebrew verbs. In verse 2 the Shepherd leads beside still waters, the leading of care that brings the sheep to rest and refreshment. In verse 3 He leads in the paths of righteousness, the leading of direction that keeps the sheep on the right way. The Shepherd does not only comfort; He directs. And He does not only direct; He comforts. Believers sometimes want one without the other: comfort without direction, or rules without rest. The Shepherd gives both, and we need both. Do I welcome His rest but resist His direction, or follow His direction but never stop to rest?
items.q: Do I welcome His rest but resist His direction, or follow His direction but never stop to rest?

items.title: The Shepherd Does Almost Everything
items.html: Count the verbs. The Shepherd makes, leads, restores, leads again, is present, comforts, prepares, anoints, fills, and pursues. The sheep lies down, walks, does not fear, and dwells. That is almost all. The Christian life rests far more on what God does than on what we do. Our part is to trust and follow. Jesus said, “He who abides in Me, and I in him, bears much fruit; for without Me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Paul wrote, “it is God who works in you both to will and to do for His good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). A tireless Shepherd cares for a flock that tires easily. Am I living the Christian life as if everything depends on me?
items.q: Am I living the Christian life as if everything depends on me?

sections.title: Through the Valley, You Are with Me

groups.title: Through the Valley, You Are with Me

items.title: The Valley Turns Theology into Prayer
items.html: In the green pastures David talks about God. In the shadow of death he talks to Him. Across the whole psalm, the move from “He” to “You” happens in the valley. Suffering made God personal. Job had a similar experience. After everything he lost and everything God said to him, he confessed, “I have heard of You by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees You” (Job 42:5). The pasture teaches us to trust the Shepherd’s gifts. The valley teaches us to trust the Shepherd Himself when the gifts are stripped away. God does not waste our valleys. Has a dark season brought me closer to God, or have I let it push me away?
items.q: Has a dark season brought me closer to God, or have I let it push me away?

items.title: Valleys Lead to Water
items.html: We would gladly skip the valleys, but in hill country the valleys are where the water runs and where grass grows green. A shepherd often has to lead his flock down through a valley to reach fresh water and new pasture. And the way to the higher hills usually runs through the valleys in between. The same is true in the life of faith. The psalm of the pilgrims to Jerusalem says, “As they pass through the Valley of Baca, they make it a spring” (Psalm 84:6). The valley was not the destination, but it was on the way, and God turned it into a place of refreshing. Valleys are needed to find water, to find fresh pasture, and to climb to higher ground. What might God be bringing me to through the valley I am in?
items.q: What might God be bringing me to through the valley I am in?

items.title: The Shepherd Walked the Valley First
items.html: Psalm 23 follows Psalm 22, the psalm Jesus quoted from the cross: “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Psalm 22:1). In that psalm the sufferer, surrounded by his attackers, says of them, “They pierced My hands and My feet” (Psalm 22:16). Zechariah foretold, “Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7), and Jesus applied those words to Himself on the night of His arrest (Matthew 26:31). The Good Shepherd went into the darkest valley alone, so that His sheep would never have to walk through one alone. Every “You are with me” in a believer’s life rests on His “Why have You forsaken Me?” Jesus was forsaken so that I could be accompanied. I never face the darkest valley alone, because He went through it first, alone, for me.
items.q: Psalm 23 follows Psalm 22, the psalm Jesus quoted from the cross: “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Psalm 22:1).

sections.title: The LORD’s Table and the LORD’s House

groups.title: The LORD’s Table and the LORD’s House

items.title: The Table Now, the House Forever
items.html: Verse 5 happens in this life: the table is set while the enemies are still present. Verse 6 reaches beyond this life: dwelling in the house of the LORD for length of days. The two belong together. The peace God gives at His table now is a foretaste of the home that is coming. Eternal life does not begin only when we die. Jesus said, “And this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent” (John 17:3). Eternal life is found in knowing Christ, and it begins the moment we come to know Him. Our fellowship with Him at His table, even with enemies watching, is an expression and a foretaste of that life. Every time God feeds me in a hard place, He is giving me a taste of forever. Am I living as if heaven is only later, or tasting it now?
items.q: Am I living as if heaven is only later, or tasting it now?

whole.title: The Shepherd’s Provision
whole.html: “I shall not want” is not an abstract promise. The rest of the psalm spells out what it means. The Shepherd provides rest and water (verse 2), restoration and guidance (verse 3), protection in the valley (verse 4), provision, honor, and abundance at the table (verse 5), and pursuit by goodness and mercy, ending in a home (verse 6). Rest, water, restoration, guidance, protection, provision, honor, abundance, pursuit, and home: there is no season of life, from green pasture to death to eternity, that falls outside the Shepherd’s care. Whatever I face, my Shepherd has provision for it.
whole.q: “I shall not want” is not an abstract promise.

whole.title: The Last Word Is the House
whole.html: Psalm 23 never pretends the path is safe. There is a dark valley, and there are enemies at the table. But the psalm places every danger between the green pastures and the house of the LORD. The last word is not “valley” or “enemies.” It is “the house of the LORD forever.” In this way the psalm mirrors the journey of a believer’s life: seasons of rest, seasons of correction, valleys, battles, and finally home. Paul could call his sufferings “our light affliction, which is but for a moment,” because it was “working for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17). Trouble is real, but it never gets the last word. God’s house does. What would change if I believed my story ends at His house?
whole.q: What would change if I believed my story ends at His house?

whole.title: Faith at Rest
whole.html: Psalm 23 asks God for nothing. There is no “lead me,” “restore me,” or “protect me.” Every line is a confession: “He leads me,” “He restores,” “You are with me.” Many psalms cry out for help, and those prayers are good and right. But Psalm 23 shows where faith can arrive: a place of rest where it simply declares what God is like and lives from trust. Paul describes the path there: “in everything by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God; and the peace of God… will guard your hearts” (Philippians 4:6–7). Psalm 23 sounds like the prayer of someone that peace has already reached. Can I spend time with God simply declaring who He is?
whole.q: Can I spend time with God simply declaring who He is?

whole.title: My Shepherd, My Cup, My Life
whole.html: Every reference to the believer in Psalm 23 is personal: “my shepherd,” “my soul,” “my head,” “my cup,” “my life.” David does not speak about God’s care for people in general. He speaks about what God is to him. Faith that stays general never touches us. It can be correct and still distant. This psalm will not let faith stay in the abstract; it must be lived out personally and change us personally. Yet the same psalm has been prayed by the whole people of God for three thousand years. Every believer who says “my” joins one flock under one Shepherd (John 10:16). Personal faith is not private faith. Is the Shepherd my Shepherd, or only someone else’s?
whole.q: Is the Shepherd my Shepherd, or only someone else’s?

whole.title: Christ and the Believer’s Whole Life
whole.html: The key words of Psalm 23 trace the whole life of a believer under the Shepherd, and each one is fulfilled in Christ. Rest: “Come to Me… and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Restoration: He brings back the wandering sheep and lays it on His shoulders (Luke 15:5). Righteousness: Christ “became for us wisdom from God—and righteousness” (1 Corinthians 1:30). Presence: “I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Abundance: “I have come that they may have life… more abundantly” (John 10:10). Pursuit: “the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10). Home: “I will come again and receive you to Myself; that where I am, there you may be also” (John 14:3). From the first day of faith to the last, there is no part of my life that Christ does not shepherd. Which of these do I most need Him to be to me today?
whole.q: Which of these do I most need Him to be to me today?

whole.title: Christ in Every Picture
whole.html: Every good thing in Psalm 23 finds its fullness in Jesus. He is the living water: “whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst” (John 4:14). His word is the path: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). He is not only the guide on the path but the path itself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). At the table we receive Him as the bread of life (John 6:35) and remember His blood in the cup. The oil of honor and refreshing points to the Holy Spirit He pours on His people. And the house of the LORD is the Father’s house He has gone to prepare (John 14:2). Psalm 23 first describes the LORD as David’s Shepherd. Read with the whole Bible, every picture leads to Jesus. When I pray this psalm, I am describing life with Him.
whole.q: Every good thing in Psalm 23 finds its fullness in Jesus.

whole.title: Israel’s Exodus in One Life
whole.html: Psalm 23 is full of wilderness language. “I shall not want” echoes “you have lacked nothing” (Deuteronomy 2:7). “He leads me” echoes “You have guided them” (Exodus 15:13). “Still waters,” waters of rest, recall the ark searching out “a resting place” (Numbers 10:33). “You prepare a table” answers “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Psalm 78:19). And the house of the LORD recalls the goal of the exodus, God’s “holy habitation” (Exodus 15:13). “You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron” (Psalm 77:20). David takes the story of a nation and makes it the testimony of one life. Every believer’s walk with God follows the same pattern: redemption, leading, provision in the desert, protection from enemies, and arrival at God’s dwelling. On the mountain of transfiguration, Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about “His decease which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31). Luke’s Greek word is the word from which we get “exodus.” Jesus is leading His people home.
whole.q: Psalm 23 is full of wilderness language.

whole.title: God Promised to Shepherd His People Himself
whole.html: Centuries after David, Israel’s leaders had failed the flock. They fed themselves, ignored the weak, and let the sheep scatter. God responded through Ezekiel: “Indeed I Myself will search for My sheep and seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11). “I will feed My flock, and I will make them lie down” (Ezekiel 34:15). He also promised, “I will establish one shepherd over them… My servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23), though David had been dead for centuries. Ezekiel 34 takes the language of Psalm 23 and turns it into a promise. Jesus claimed that promise: “I am the good shepherd… and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:11, 16). He is both the LORD who shepherds His people Himself and the Son of David. When human leaders fail us, God Himself comes to shepherd His people. Have I let the failures of human shepherds make me doubt the Good Shepherd?
whole.q: Have I let the failures of human shepherds make me doubt the Good Shepherd?

whole.title: The Lamb Who Is the Shepherd
whole.html: At the end of the Bible the roles meet in one Person. John sees that “the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and lead them to living fountains of waters. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 7:17). The Shepherd became a sheep. Isaiah described Him as “led as a lamb to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7). The One who shepherds us knows from the inside what it is to be a sheep: to be weak, to be led, to face the slaughter. He does not shepherd from a distance. He leads His people to the waters He once went without, and He wipes away tears He Himself has cried. I can trust a Shepherd who has been a Lamb.
whole.q: At the end of the Bible the roles meet in one Person.

whole.title: David Failed as a Shepherd; Christ Never Does
whole.html: David, the shepherd-king, knew his own failures. Nathan exposed his sin with a story about a rich man who stole a poor man’s only lamb, and then said, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). Later, after David’s proud census brought a plague on Israel, he cried out, “Surely I have sinned… but these sheep, what have they done?” (2 Samuel 24:17). Perhaps that is part of why David wrote as a sheep. Even the best human shepherd needs a Shepherd. Pastors fail. Parents fail. Leaders fail. Christ never fails His flock. He did not take the poor man’s lamb; He became the Lamb. He did not bring death on the sheep; He bore it for them. When the shepherds in my life have failed me, or when I have failed those I shepherd, I can run to the one Shepherd who never will.
whole.q: David, the shepherd-king, knew his own failures.

whole.title: A Psalm for Every Stage, Not Only Funerals
whole.html: Psalm 23 is read at gravesides more than almost any other passage, and rightly so. It gives comfort to the dying and to those who mourn. But it is not only a funeral psalm. It covers the whole of life: seasons of rest, times of wandering and restoration, dark valleys, battles, celebrations, and finally death and the home beyond. A young believer needs “He leads me” as much as a dying saint needs “I will fear no evil.” The Shepherd is with His people at every stage, not just the last one. If I save this psalm for funerals, I miss the Shepherd’s care for my ordinary days. Which line of Psalm 23 do I most need for the stage of life I am in now?
whole.q: Which line of Psalm 23 do I most need for the stage of life I am in now?

whole.title: Cross, Shepherd, Crown
whole.html:
Some Bible readers have noticed a pattern in Psalms 22, 23, and 24. Psalm 22 describes the suffering of the cross. Psalm 23 describes the Shepherd’s care. Psalm 24 calls the gates to open for “the King of glory” (Psalm 24:7). Read together, they move from the cross to the Shepherd to the crown. The psalms do not announce this as their structure, and it should be treated as a devotional pattern rather than the plan of the text. But it is a helpful way to see the Shepherd’s work in Christ. He died for His sheep, He shepherds them now, and He will reign in glory.

Psalm 23. The whole psalm is the testimony of a life kept by the Shepherd. David, the shepherd who became a king, looks back and confesses that the LORD has been his Shepherd all along: in green pastures and on right paths, in the darkest valley, at a table set before enemies, and all the way to the house of the LORD. In the valley he stops talking about God and starts talking to Him. Read with the rest of Scripture, every picture opens onto the life of a believer with Jesus, the Good Shepherd, who gives rest, restores, corrects in love, welcomes us to His table, fills us with His Spirit, pursues us with goodness and mercy, and brings us home.

What God may be saying: “I am your Shepherd. You belong to Me. Let Me lead you to rest, bring you back when you wander, and walk with you through every valley. You do not have to wait for your battles to end to sit at My table. My goodness and mercy are following you all your days, and I am bringing you home.”
whole.q: Some Bible readers have noticed a pattern in Psalms 22, 23, and 24.

1.brief: In this psalm of David, the shepherd who became Israel’s king confesses that the LORD is his own Shepherd, a title kings bore for their people and Scripture gives to God Himself, so that under His care David lacks nothing he truly needs. Every believer may make the same personal confession, because the LORD who shepherded David shepherds His people through Jesus, the Good Shepherd (John 10:11).
1.explain:
“A Psalm of David.”

The title names David as the author of the psalm but gives no occasion for it. That matters, because the man who wrote these lines had spent his youth with sheep. He kept his father’s flock, and when a lion or a bear took a lamb, he went after it and rescued the lamb from its mouth (1 Samuel 17:34–35). Later the LORD took him “from the sheepfolds” to shepherd His people Israel (Psalm 78:70–71). The psalm reads as the settled trust of a man looking back over a life spent under the LORD’s care and looking ahead to His house. Episodes from David’s story help us hear these words on his lips, but none of them is named as the setting, and the psalm was given for every worshiper who prays it.

“The LORD is my shepherd;”

The psalm opens with the divine name, “The LORD,” the God who made Himself known to Israel and bound Himself to His people. Joined to that name is a title with royal weight. Rulers in the ancient world were called shepherds of their people, and the LORD Himself told David, “You shall shepherd My people Israel” (2 Samuel 5:2). Scripture gives the same title to God: Jacob spoke of “the Mighty God of Jacob (From there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel)” (Genesis 49:24), and Asaph prayed, “Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel” (Psalm 80:1). So the shepherd who became king confesses that he is himself a sheep, and that the LORD is his Shepherd.

The little word “my” makes the confession personal. A shepherd owned his flock, fed it, led it, and defended it, and the sheep depended on him for everything. David is not describing God from a distance. He is saying to whom he belongs and who takes responsibility for him.

Read through the rest of Scripture, this confession belongs to every believer. The LORD promised His scattered flock, “Indeed I Myself will search for My sheep and seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11), and Jesus declared, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives His life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Psalm 23 does not name Jesus, but the LORD who shepherded David is the One who shepherds His people through Him.

“I shall not want.”

To “want” here means to lack or to be without. Because the LORD is his Shepherd, David lacks nothing he truly needs. Moses used the same word of Israel’s forty years in the wilderness: “These forty years the LORD your God has been with you; you have lacked nothing” (Deuteronomy 2:7). A barren wilderness was no place to find plenty, yet God’s people lacked nothing there because He was with them. David’s confidence likewise rests on the Shepherd, not on easy circumstances.

The line confesses sufficiency under the Shepherd’s care. It does not promise every desire, wealth, or a life without hardship; within a few lines the same psalm speaks of a dark valley and of enemies. What it does promise is that the sheep of this Shepherd will have what the Shepherd knows they need. Everything that follows in the psalm unfolds this opening line.
1.notes:
In Hebrew the line reads YHWH ro‘i lo’ ’echsar, literally “The LORD my shepherd, I shall not lack.” Ro‘i is a participle of the verb ra‘ah, “to pasture” or “to tend,” with the suffix “my.” The familiar title YHWH-Rohi, “the LORD my Shepherd,” comes from this line. It is a confession drawn from Psalm 23 rather than a compound name that appears elsewhere in Scripture.

The Hebrew verb translated “want” means “to lack” and is the same word used in Deuteronomy 2:7 and Nehemiah 9:21 to describe how Israel lacked nothing during the forty years in the wilderness.

Kings were commonly called shepherds in the ancient Near East. In L. W. King’s English translation of the Code of Hammurabi, the Babylonian king calls himself “the shepherd of the oppressed and of the slaves” in the prologue and “the salvation-bearing shepherd, whose staff is straight” in the epilogue.

The superscription “A Psalm of David” stands at the head of verse 1 in the NKJV, and the Hebrew Bible also counts the title as part of verse 1 here. Psalm 23 therefore has the same verse numbers in Hebrew and English.

The NLT renders the second line “I have all that I need,” expressing positively what the Hebrew states as a negative.

hearing.observe: The heading, “A Psalm of David,” changes how we hear the first line. David knew shepherding from the inside. He was out keeping his father’s sheep when Samuel came to anoint him (1 Samuel 16:11). He fought a lion and a bear to rescue a lamb from their mouths (1 Samuel 17:34–36). God took him “from the sheepfolds” to shepherd His people Israel (Psalm 78:70–71). Yet when David writes this psalm, he does not speak as the shepherd. He speaks as the sheep. The man who had protected flocks and then ruled a nation knew he still needed the same care he had given to others.
hearing.hear: If David, the shepherd-king, called himself a sheep, then I will never become too strong, too experienced, or too important to need my Shepherd. Whatever responsibility I carry for others, I am still one of His flock. I don’t have to pretend I have outgrown my need for Him. I can lay down the weight of being in charge and let Him lead me.

hearing.observe: David could have said “a shepherd” or “our shepherd,” and both would be true. Israel sang, “We are the people of His pasture, and the sheep of His hand” (Psalm 95:7). But here David says “my.” The God who led the whole nation through the wilderness is personally the Shepherd of one man. Spurgeon called this “the sweetest word of the whole.” Without it, the line is a true statement about God. With it, the line becomes a confession of belonging. Jesus speaks the same way about His flock: “I know My sheep, and am known by My own” (John 10:14).
hearing.hear: The LORD is not only a shepherd in general. He is my Shepherd. It is possible to believe that God cares for His people and never rest in His care for me. This verse invites me to say “my.” He knows me by name, even on the days I am a mystery to myself, and He has taken responsibility for me. What a sweet thing to hear: I belong to Him, and He belongs to me.

hearing.observe: “I shall not want” uses the same Hebrew word Moses used at the end of Israel’s wilderness years: “These forty years the LORD your God has been with you; you have lacked nothing” (Deuteronomy 2:7). Nehemiah later says it again: “Forty years You sustained them in the wilderness; they lacked nothing” (Nehemiah 9:21). The wilderness was dry, hot, and dangerous, yet Israel could testify that nothing essential had been missing. David takes the nation’s testimony and speaks it over his own life. This is not a promise that every desire will be met, since the same psalm includes a dark valley and enemies. It means the sheep will not lack what the Shepherd knows it needs.
hearing.hear: Under the Lord’s care, I will not lack what I truly need, even in a dry and difficult season. When something I want is missing, I can trust that my Shepherd knows whether I need it today. “My God shall supply all your need” (Philippians 4:19). I can stop measuring His care by my wish list and start trusting it because of who He is.

reflections.title: The King Who Was a Shepherd
reflections.html: David was the shepherd who became a king. Jesus is the King who came as a Shepherd. Micah promised that a ruler would come out of Bethlehem, David’s hometown, and that He would “stand and feed His flock in the strength of the LORD” (Micah 5:4). When the wise men asked where the King of the Jews would be born, the scribes answered with that promise: “Out of you shall come a Ruler who will shepherd My people Israel” (Matthew 2:6). In Jesus the crown and the shepherd’s staff are held by the same hands. He rules by caring for His flock, and He shepherds with the authority of a King. Some want Jesus as a gentle Shepherd but not as King. Others bow to Him as King but never let Him care for them. He is both. Have I let Jesus be both my King and my Shepherd?
reflections.q: Have I let Jesus be both my King and my Shepherd?

reflections.title: Leaders Must First Be Led
reflections.html: David shepherded a nation, yet in this psalm he places himself among the sheep. Every leader in God’s house is first a member of the flock. Peter, an apostle who had walked with Jesus, wrote to church elders as “a fellow elder.” He told them to “shepherd the flock of God which is among you,” and he reminded them that the reward would come “when the Chief Shepherd appears” (1 Peter 5:1–4). A leader who is not being led will drive people with his own strength, anxieties, or ambition. Pastors, parents, ministry leaders, and employers all shepherd someone. We can only give what we are receiving. The leaders who care for people best are the ones who still lie down in His pastures, still need restoring, and still follow His voice. Am I leading others out of my own walk with the Shepherd, or out of my own strength?
reflections.q: Am I leading others out of my own walk with the Shepherd, or out of my own strength?

reflections.title: The Shepherd Who Gives His Life
reflections.html: The LORD who shepherded David has a face and a name: Jesus. “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives His life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Jesus then draws a contrast: a hired hand “sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees” (John 10:12), because the sheep are not his own. The Good Shepherd does the opposite. He walks toward the wolf, and it costs Him His life. Then the Father raised Him from the dead as “that great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant” (Hebrews 13:20). David could say “The LORD is my shepherd.” We can say the same and add what David could only glimpse: my Shepherd died for me and lives to lead me. No one who has been loved like that is an unwanted sheep.
reflections.q: The LORD who shepherded David has a face and a name: Jesus.

reflections.title: Looking Back, I Did Not Lack
reflections.html: “I shall not want” can be said looking forward in faith, but it can also be said looking back over a whole life. Many older believers can trace God’s hand through years they did not understand at the time. The job they did not get, the door that closed, the thing they begged for and never received: they now see they did not need it. Moses told Israel that God “humbled you, allowed you to hunger, and fed you with manna… that He might make you know that man shall not live by bread alone” (Deuteronomy 8:3). Even the hunger was part of His care. At the end of his life Joshua told the nation that “not one thing has failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spoke concerning you” (Joshua 23:14). The things we thought we wanted were often things we did not need. What am I demanding from God now that I may one day thank Him for withholding?
reflections.q: What am I demanding from God now that I may one day thank Him for withholding?

reflections.title: The LORD Is Named Before the Sheep
reflections.html: In Hebrew, the very first word of the psalm after the heading is God’s covenant name, YHWH, the LORD. Before David says anything about himself, his needs, or his journey, he names the God who revealed Himself to Moses as “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14). The comfort of Psalm 23 does not rest on the beauty of the picture but on the identity of the Shepherd. And the eternal I AM takes up one of the humblest jobs in the ancient world. Shepherding was dirty, tiring, and lowly work; Joseph told his brothers that “every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians” (Genesis 46:34). The God who needs nothing stoops to care for creatures who need everything. My peace rests on who God is before it rests on anything He gives me. When I start with my need, I spiral. When I start with His name, I can rest.
reflections.q: In Hebrew, the very first word of the psalm after the heading is God’s covenant name, YHWH, the LORD.

reflections.title: Yahweh-Rohi: The LORD My Shepherd
reflections.html: Many believers know this Hebrew line as one of the names of God: Yahweh-Rohi (often written Jehovah-Rohi), “The LORD is my Shepherd.” Scripture also records Jehovah-Jireh, “The-LORD-Will-Provide,” the name Abraham gave the mountain where God provided the ram (Genesis 22:14), and Jehovah-Shalom, the name Gideon gave his altar (Judges 6:24). Those names were attached to places. This one rises out of a life. David knew a shepherd’s care from his own years with the flock. Here he confesses his own dependence on the LORD. A name like this is learned by walking with Him. Every believer who has been fed, led, restored, and carried can make it his own confession. What has God shown Himself to be in my life?
reflections.q: What has God shown Himself to be in my life?

reflections.title: A Settled Question Settles Anxiety
reflections.html: The opening line has no verb in Hebrew. It reads simply, “The LORD, my shepherd.” There is no “if,” no “maybe,” and no “I hope so.” David does not write this as a wish; he states it as a settled fact, and its certainty rests on God’s character rather than on David’s feelings. Paul spoke with the same settledness: “I know whom I have believed and am persuaded that He is able to keep what I have committed to Him until that Day” (2 Timothy 1:12). Much of our anxiety lives in one unsettled question: “Will God really take care of me?” As long as that question stays open, every need feels like a threat. Jesus answers it plainly: “your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (Matthew 6:32). When the question is settled, anxiety loses its footing. The valley may still come, but the psalm starts on solid ground. Have I settled the question of whether the LORD is my Shepherd?
reflections.q: Have I settled the question of whether the LORD is my Shepherd?

reflections.title: To Say “My Shepherd” Is to Admit “I Am a Sheep.”
reflections.html: Every confession of the LORD as Shepherd carries a second confession inside it: I am a sheep. Sheep depend on the shepherd for protection, direction, and water. To call Him Shepherd is to give up the claim that I can manage my own life. “You are not your own,” Paul wrote; “you were bought at a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). We cannot keep our independence and claim His provision at the same time. Self-reliance looks strong, but it produces anxiety, because everything depends on me. Trust produces rest, because everything depends on Him. The poverty of a sheep turns out to be its wealth, because it has nothing to protect and everything to receive. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3). Where am I still trying to be my own shepherd?
reflections.q: Where am I still trying to be my own shepherd?

reflections.title: The Shepherd of Jacob
reflections.html: The first person in Scripture to speak of God as his shepherd was Jacob, a man whose story is marked by deceit and wandering. Near the end of his life he blessed Joseph’s sons in the name of “the God who has fed me all my life long to this day” (Genesis 48:15). The word “fed” is the Hebrew word for shepherding. Later he called the LORD “the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel” (Genesis 49:24). Jacob had cheated his brother, run from home, been cheated in return, and limped away from a night of wrestling with God. He had not earned God’s care. Looking back, he saw that God had been shepherding him the whole time, and Hebrews remembers this very moment as an act of faith: “By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph” (Hebrews 11:21). Jacob’s faith was real, but it rested on a Shepherd who had held on to him long before he deserved it. The shepherd title for God was born in the life of a wanderer. God shepherds the undeserving and the wandering, not only the faithful. If He could shepherd Jacob all his life long, He can shepherd me.
reflections.q: The first person in Scripture to speak of God as his shepherd was Jacob, a man whose story is marked by deceit and wandering.

2.brief: The Shepherd makes David lie down in green pastures and leads him beside still waters, literally waters of rest, so that rest and refreshment come from the Shepherd’s leading rather than the sheep’s own searching. Read through the rest of Scripture, this is the rest Christ gives to those who come to Him (Matthew 11:29).
2.explain:
“He makes me to lie down in green pastures;”

The verb is causative: the shepherd brings the sheep to a place where it can lie down. A sheep settles when it has eaten and feels safe, so the picture is of a flock fed and at rest. “Green pastures” are meadows of fresh, tender grass, valuable in a dry land where good grazing could not be taken for granted. David had led flocks through the hills around Bethlehem and knew how much depended on a shepherd who knew where to find it. The sheep does not discover the pasture on its own; the Shepherd leads it there and settles it down. Rest is His gift before it is the sheep’s experience.

“He leads me beside the still waters.”

The Hebrew reads literally “waters of rest.” These are waters where the flock can drink and lie down, a quiet place of refreshment rather than a rushing torrent. The verb “leads” describes guiding a flock to a watering place and letting it rest there. Again the Shepherd is the one who acts. Together the two lines picture the daily needs of the flock, food, water, and rest, supplied by the Shepherd’s leading rather than by the sheep’s own searching.

Read through the rest of Scripture, this rest points to the rest Christ gives. He called, “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest,” and promised, “you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:28–29). The weary believer is brought to rest the same way David was: by following the Shepherd who leads.
2.notes:
“Green pastures” combines a word for a pasture or meadow with deshe’, fresh or tender grass. The KJV margin renders the phrase “pastures of tender grass.”

The Hebrew behind “still waters” is me menuchot. The noun menuchah means rest or a resting place. It is the word in Psalm 95:11, “They shall not enter My rest,” and in Psalm 116:7, “Return to your rest, O my soul.”

The verb translated “leads” in this line is nahal. Isaiah 40:11 uses it of the LORD who will “gently lead those who are with young,” and Isaiah 49:10 of the One who will guide His people “by the springs of water.”

“Makes me to lie down” is the Hiphil of rabats, a verb often used of animals lying at rest. The LORD uses the same form in Ezekiel 34:15: “I will feed My flock, and I will make them lie down.”

The NLT reads “He lets me rest in green meadows; he leads me beside peaceful streams.”

hearing.observe: Both verbs in this verse belong to the Shepherd: “He makes me to lie down,” and “He leads me.” The sheep does not find its own rest. “Makes me to lie down” describes the Shepherd bringing the sheep to the place of rest and settling it there. Spurgeon observed that many people know about God’s blessings but cannot lie down in them. In this verse rest is not something the sheep produces. It is the Shepherd’s work. And sometimes “makes” is exactly the right word, because a restless sheep may have to be stopped before it will rest.
hearing.hear: I cannot make myself rest. Fear, conflict, and hunger for more keep me on my feet. This verse invites me to let the Shepherd lead me to rest instead of trying to produce it myself. Sometimes He “makes” me lie down through an illness, a closed door, or a pause I did not choose. In those moments I want to remember that His stopping me can be His care. He knows what I need before I do.

hearing.observe: The rest this verse describes is the rest Jesus offers. He said, “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest,” and promised that those who come to Him “will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:28–29). As in Psalm 23, the rest is given by the Shepherd, not earned by the sheep. At the end of the Bible the picture is still the same: “the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and lead them to living fountains of waters” (Revelation 7:17).
hearing.hear: Jesus is still saying, “Come to Me.” My weariness is not a reason to stay away from Him. It is the reason to come. I can bring Him the heavy load I am carrying today and receive the rest He promised. And I can look forward to the day He leads me to living fountains of water, where my soul will never be weary again.

reflections.title: What Keeps a Sheep on Its Feet
reflections.html: Phillip Keller, who worked as a shepherd and wrote about this psalm, observed that sheep will not lie down unless four things are true: they are free from fear, free from friction with other sheep, free from pests, and free from hunger. Only the shepherd can provide all four. Whether or not every flock behaves this way, the picture fits our souls closely. Fear keeps us alert and restless, and God answers it with His presence: “Fear not, for I am with you” (Isaiah 41:10). Friction in our relationships keeps us tense, and the Shepherd makes peace within His flock. Small irritations wear us down until we cannot settle. Hunger for something more keeps us roaming. “He makes me to lie down” means the Shepherd deals with each of these. Rest is not the absence of a busy schedule; it is the presence of a Shepherd who has handled what keeps us on our feet. Which of these four is keeping me from lying down?
reflections.q: Which of these four is keeping me from lying down?

reflections.title: Rest Comes Before the Road
reflections.html: The first thing the Shepherd does is make the sheep lie down. The paths do not come until verse 3. Scripture follows this order again and again. Adam was created on the sixth day, so his first full day was the day God rested. Israel was redeemed from Egypt before they received the law at Sinai. Jesus said, “I will give you rest” before He said, “Take My yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:28–29). God’s people work from rest, not toward it. Many believers live the other way around. They try to finish the path so they can finally earn some rest, and they never arrive. The Shepherd begins with the green pasture. Am I trying to earn the rest God wants to give me first?
reflections.q: Am I trying to earn the rest God wants to give me first?

reflections.title: Why We Will Not Lie Down
reflections.html: Often what keeps us from God’s rest is not our circumstances but our own hearts. Busyness can hide a quiet pride, a belief that things will fall apart without us. Yet “He who keeps Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4), and “He gives His beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). Going to sleep each night can be a small act of faith, a confession that God stays awake. Noise and distraction crowd out the stillness in which we listen best: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). Sometimes we refuse to rest until we have answers, but the Shepherd gives rest through His nearness, not through explanations. What is my reason for not lying down?
reflections.q: What is my reason for not lying down?

reflections.title: Waters of Rest
reflections.html: “Still waters” is literally “waters of rests.” The Hebrew word (menuchot) means rest or a resting place. Naomi used it when she prayed that Ruth would find “rest” in a new home (Ruth 1:9). The ark of the covenant went ahead of Israel “to search out a resting place for them” (Numbers 10:33). Most strikingly, God uses the word for His own rest: “This is My resting place forever; here I will dwell” (Psalm 132:14). The Shepherd does not lead His sheep to a nervous, temporary pause. He leads them into the kind of rest God Himself enjoys. Hebrews says, “There remains therefore a rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). The quiet waters are a taste of God’s own Sabbath. Do I expect God’s rest to be a short break, or a share in His own peace?
reflections.q: Do I expect God’s rest to be a short break, or a share in His own peace?

reflections.title: He Leads; He Does Not Drive
reflections.html: “He leads me” uses a Hebrew verb (nahal) that pictures a shepherd gently guiding his flock to water. The same verb describes God guiding His redeemed people out of Egypt: “You have guided them in Your strength to Your holy habitation” (Exodus 15:13). Isaiah uses it of the Shepherd who will “gently lead those who are with young” (Isaiah 40:11). Jacob, a lifelong shepherd, understood this. When Esau wanted to travel together, Jacob answered that the children were weak and the flocks were nursing, “and if the men should drive them hard one day, all the flock will die.” He promised instead to “lead on slowly at a pace which the livestock… and the children, are able to endure” (Genesis 33:13–14). Whatever else Jacob intended, he knew that sheep are led, not driven. Jesus’ sheep follow Him because “they know his voice” (John 10:4). Christ does not drive His people by fear. He goes ahead of them and draws them by love. Am I following a gentle Shepherd, or a harsh one I have imagined?
reflections.q: Am I following a gentle Shepherd, or a harsh one I have imagined?

reflections.title: Green Pastures on a Galilean Hillside
reflections.html: Green pastures are real provision: good food in a land where grass was often scarce. Spurgeon applied them to the Scriptures, where God feeds His people. That is a fair application, though not the plain meaning. Mark records a scene that seems to echo the psalm. Jesus saw a great crowd and “was moved with compassion for them, because they were like sheep not having a shepherd.” He taught them, then commanded them to “sit down in groups on the green grass,” and fed them until “they all ate and were filled” (Mark 6:34, 39, 42). Mark may intend the echo: the Shepherd of Psalm 23 has come, making His sheep lie down in green pastures. He cared for their hearts and their stomachs. God cares for the whole person. Do I bring Him only my spiritual needs, or my whole life?
reflections.q: Do I bring Him only my spiritual needs, or my whole life?

3.brief: The LORD revives David’s whole weary life and leads him on right paths, tracks that go where the Shepherd intends and keep him in what is right before God, and He does so “for His name’s sake,” for the honor of His own character. Spiritually, the Shepherd restores believers who have fallen or wandered, as He restored David after his sin, and His guidance rests on His faithfulness rather than on the sheep’s performance.
3.explain:
“He restores my soul;”

In the Old Testament the “soul” is the whole living person, not a separate compartment inside a person. To “restore” it is to bring it back, to renew and revive it. David is speaking of the Shepherd reviving a weary or failing life, the way a worn-out sheep is brought back to strength. The same words can suggest bringing back a sheep that has wandered, though in David’s picture the main thought is renewal.

Read through the rest of Scripture, the Shepherd also restores believers who have fallen or wandered, as He restored David himself after his sin. When Nathan confronted him, David confessed, “I have sinned against the LORD,” and Nathan answered, “The LORD also has put away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13). David’s prayer of repentance asks, “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation” (Psalm 51:12).

“He leads me in the paths of righteousness”

The word “paths” describes tracks or well-worn trails. A shepherd leads the flock along tracks that go somewhere, the right way through rough and unfamiliar country. “Righteousness” first describes paths that are right, true and reliable, leading where the Shepherd intends. In Israel’s vocabulary the word also carries its moral sense of what is right before God. The Shepherd keeps David on the road that reaches its goal, and on that road David walks in what pleases God.

“For His name’s sake.”

God’s “name” is His revealed character and reputation. The Shepherd leads this way because of who He is and for the honor of His own name. That gives David’s security a firm foundation. The LORD’s guidance does not rest on how well the sheep performs; it rests on His faithfulness to Himself. David prays on the same ground elsewhere: “For You are my rock and my fortress; Therefore, for Your name’s sake, Lead me and guide me” (Psalm 31:3).
3.notes:
“Restores” translates the Polel form of shuv, the common verb for turning or returning. Lamentations 1:16 uses another form of the same verb with the same noun, nephesh, for the comforter “who should restore my life.”

“Paths” translates ma‘gal. Proverbs 4:11 uses the same word: “I have led you in right paths.” The Hebrew phrase here is literally “tracks of righteousness.” The ESV, NIV, and NASB keep “paths of righteousness,” and the NLT reads “right paths.”

The NLT renders the first line “He renews my strength,” taking “soul” in its sense of the whole person’s life and vigor.

hearing.observe: The order of this verse matters. First, “He restores my soul.” Then, “He leads me in the paths of righteousness.” Restoration comes before direction. A worn-out or fallen sheep cannot follow a path. It must first be brought back and set on its feet; only then can it walk the right way. God does not demand righteous living from a soul He has not first restored. David prayed in this order after his great sin: “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation… Then I will teach transgressors Your ways” (Psalm 51:12–13). Grace comes first, and obedience follows.
hearing.hear: The Lord does not wait for me to fix myself before He helps me. On the days I feel worn out or far away, I don’t have to clean myself up before I come to Him. He restores first, then He leads. That makes me want to follow His paths gladly, not anxiously, because I am walking in strength He has given back to me.

hearing.observe: “He restores my soul” reaches deeper than renewed energy. The Hebrew word for “soul” (nephesh) means the whole living person, and the verb means to bring back. The Shepherd is not touching up the surface of a life. He reaches its deepest weariness and wandering and brings the whole person back. His restoring is also personal. David says “my soul,” not “the flock.” The Shepherd knows exactly what is broken in each sheep and where. And He restores for a purpose: the restored sheep can walk again, follow Him, and live the life He intends.
hearing.hear: I often want God to fix something on the surface: a situation, a mood, a problem that is in my way. He wants to restore me deeply. I can let Him reach the places I would rather keep covered, because He means to heal what is broken, not just help me feel better for a day. What He restores, He restores so I can follow Him.

hearing.observe: “Paths of righteousness” are literally right tracks, well-worn ways that lead where they should. God called His people to “ask for the old paths, where the good way is, and walk in it” (Jeremiah 6:16). Righteousness here means what is right in God’s eyes, and the Shepherd is the one who chooses the path. A sheep left to itself will wander after whatever looks greener. The path is right because it is His path, and He leads on it “for His name’s sake.” It is not always the easy way. The very next verse leads through a dark valley.
hearing.hear: The Lord leads me toward what is right in His eyes, not toward where I think I should be led. I often have my own idea of what the right path looks like: easier, quicker, more comfortable. I can stop insisting on my own map and follow the One who knows the way. When He leads, the path is right, even when it is hard.

reflections.title: “Restores” Means “Brings Back.”
reflections.html: “He restores my soul” could be translated, “He brings my soul back.” The Hebrew verb (shuv) is the root of the Old Testament language of repentance and return. Ephraim prayed, “Restore me, and I will return” (Jeremiah 31:18). Israel prayed after the fall of Jerusalem, “Turn us back to You, O LORD, and we will be restored” (Lamentations 5:21). In both prayers the turning begins with God. Repentance is first something the Shepherd does for the sheep before it is something the sheep does. Jesus told of a shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine, goes after the one, and carries it home on his shoulders (Luke 15:4–6). Peter wrote to believers, “you were like sheep going astray, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25). “The goodness of God leads you to repentance” (Romans 2:4). If I have wandered, my way back begins with His reach toward me.
reflections.q: “He restores my soul” could be translated, “He brings my soul back.”

reflections.title: The Cast-Down Sheep
reflections.html: Shepherds speak of a “cast” sheep, one that has rolled onto its back and cannot get up again. Left alone, it can die. The shepherd’s job is to find it, roll it over, and hold it steady until it can stand. The Psalms speak of the soul in the same condition: “Why are you cast down, O my soul?… Hope in God” (Psalm 42:5). This shepherding picture illustrates the verse; it is not what the Hebrew word itself means. But it fits. Some believers are not rebelling; they are simply down and cannot get up. They have been knocked over by grief, exhaustion, or failure. The Shepherd does not scold a cast sheep. He lifts it back onto its feet. If I am down today, I can let Him lift me. If someone else is down, I can treat them the way the Shepherd does.
reflections.q: Shepherds speak of a “cast” sheep, one that has rolled onto its back and cannot get up again.

reflections.title: For His Name’s Sake
reflections.html: The Shepherd leads His sheep “for His name’s sake.” A shepherd whose flock was lost or starving would be disgraced, so God has tied His own honor to the care of His people. “For My name’s sake I will defer My anger” (Isaiah 48:9). “I do not do this for your sake, O house of Israel, but for My holy name’s sake” (Ezekiel 36:22). If God’s care depended on our faithfulness, it would be as fragile as we are. Because it rests on His name, it is as steady as He is. “If we are faithless, He remains faithful; He cannot deny Himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). Even the righteousness of the path is His gift. Jeremiah foretold a King whose name would be “THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS” (Jeremiah 23:6). My security rests on His character, not on my record. Am I trusting my track record, or His name?
reflections.q: Am I trusting my track record, or His name?

4.brief: Even in the valley of the shadow of death, a place of real and deadly danger, David will fear no evil, and here he turns from speaking about the LORD to speaking to Him: “For You are with me.” The rod that defended the flock and the staff that supported and guided it comfort him, and read through the rest of Scripture they speak of the Shepherd’s loving discipline and guidance of His people, as Hebrews 12:6 shows.
4.explain:
“Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death,”

The road now leads down into a “valley,” a deep ravine where light is poor and danger can hide. The NKJV keeps the traditional rendering “the shadow of death.” The Hebrew word describes deep darkness, and Scripture often links that darkness with death and mortal danger (Job 10:21–22; 38:17). On either understanding, this is a place of real and potentially deadly threat. Death is certainly within the valley, but it is not limited to the hour of dying; it covers every dark stretch of life where danger presses close.

The words “walk through” assume passage. David expects to keep moving and to come out on the other side. The Shepherd leads into the valley, and He leads through it.

“I will fear no evil;”

“Evil” here means harm or calamity of any kind. David does not pretend the danger is unreal; he refuses to be ruled by fear of it. The next words give the reason.

“For You are with me;”

Here David turns from speaking about the LORD to speaking to Him. Until now he has said “He”; now he says “You.” In the darkest part of the road David addresses his Shepherd directly, and this line stands at the heart of the psalm. His courage rests on the Shepherd’s presence, not on escape. The LORD does not promise to keep David out of the valley; He is with him in it.

“Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.”

The “rod” was a short, heavy club the shepherd carried to drive off wild animals; the same word can name a ruler’s scepter. The “staff” was a longer stick for walking, for guiding the flock, and for supporting a sheep in difficult ground. Both belong to the Shepherd, “Your rod and Your staff,” and both “comfort” David, because they show that his Shepherd is equipped and ready to protect and guide him.

Read through the rest of Scripture, the rod speaks of the Shepherd’s authority and loving discipline, and the staff of His guidance and support. The prophets picture God claiming His flock under the rod: “I will make you pass under the rod” (Ezekiel 20:37). Hebrews says, “For whom the LORD loves He chastens” (Hebrews 12:6). Because David says these things comfort him, the discipline in view is the reassuring care of a Shepherd who will not let His sheep be lost, never harshness or threat.
4.notes:
“The shadow of death” translates tsalmawet. The traditional understanding divides the word into tsel, “shadow,” and mawet, “death,” and the Septuagint, the Targum, and the Syriac all render it that way. Many Hebrew scholars instead read a single noun meaning “deep darkness,” formed from a root meaning to be dark. Amos 5:8, where the LORD “turns the shadow of death into morning,” uses the word for the darkness of night. Both readings describe a place of mortal danger.

“Valley” translates gai’. Isaiah 9:2 uses tsalmawet for “the land of the shadow of death.” The ESV, NIV, and NASB keep “the valley of the shadow of death”; the NLT reads “the darkest valley.”

“Rod” translates shebet, which can also mean a tribe. Micah 7:14, “Shepherd Your people with Your staff,” uses the same word for the shepherd’s implement, and Leviticus 27:32 speaks of the animals of the flock that pass “under the rod” to be counted for the tithe.

“Staff” translates mish‘enet, from a verb meaning to lean on. Elsewhere it is a walking stick, as in Exodus 21:19, “walks about outside with his staff,” and Zechariah 8:4, “Each one with his staff in his hand.”

In Hebrew, verse 4 uses the independent pronoun ’attah, “You,” followed by “Your rod and Your staff,” and the direct address continues through verse 5. The verb “comfort” is from nacham in its form meaning to console.

hearing.observe: In verses 1–3 David speaks about the LORD: “He makes… He leads… He restores.” In verse 4 the psalm turns: “For You are with me.” In the darkest place, David stops talking about God and starts talking to Him. Green pastures produced a description; the valley produced a conversation. Jesus did the same in His darkest hour. On the cross, even as He felt forsaken, He still cried, “My God, My God” (Matthew 27:46).
hearing.hear: The place where I am most afraid can become the place where I am closest to God. When I walk through a dark season, I don’t have to stand at a distance and talk about Him. I can talk to Him. My valley can turn what I know about God into real prayer.

hearing.observe: David does not say the valley is safe. He says, “I will fear no evil.” The danger is real, and he walks through it, not around it. His courage does not come from denying the darkness or from sheer willpower. It comes from a Person: “for You are with me.” The Shepherd does not always lift His sheep out of the valley. More often He walks with them through it. He may not explain the darkness, but He gives His presence in it. “God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind” (2 Timothy 1:7).
hearing.hear: I don’t have to pretend the danger isn’t real. My courage can rest on God being with me in it. I may never get an explanation for this valley, but I have His presence, and His presence is enough for me to keep walking without being ruled by fear.

hearing.observe: “You are with me” is fulfilled for believers today by the Holy Spirit. Before He went to the cross, Jesus promised “another Helper, that He may abide with you forever,” and then said, “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you” (John 14:16, 18). Scripture shows the Spirit doing the Shepherd’s work. He leads God’s children (Romans 8:14), and Isaiah says of Israel in the wilderness, “the Spirit of the LORD causes him to rest” (Isaiah 63:14). Psalm 23 does not mention the Spirit, but the rest of Scripture shows how the Shepherd’s presence stays with His sheep now.
hearing.hear: I am not alone in my valley. Jesus has not left me an orphan. By His Spirit He is with me now, as near in the dark as He was in the green pastures. When I feel alone, I can ask the Holy Spirit to make His presence real to me and remind me that I belong to Him.

hearing.observe: “The shadow of death” translates one Hebrew word (tsalmavet) that can also be read “deep darkness.” It describes the darkest places a person can walk, and those places are not only physical death. Many valleys feel like death: a marriage that is failing, health that is slipping away, a dream or a ministry that seems to be dying, a season of grief that will not lift. The One who says “I am with you” at the end of life is with His people in every dying thing along the way. Jesus Himself went down into the low places. He was “a Man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3), and He is not ashamed to walk with His sheep there.
hearing.hear: Christ is with me in the low places of my life and in the seasons when things around me are dying. I don’t have to wait until my last day to need this verse. When something I love is ending, I can say, “You are with me,” and know that the Man of sorrows understands, and that He will lead me through.

hearing.observe: “Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.” The rod was a short club for driving off predators and for correcting and counting the sheep. The staff was a longer stick for guiding, supporting, and lifting. It may seem strange that a tool of correction brings comfort, but notice the word “Your.” These are the Shepherd’s own tools in the Shepherd’s own hand. In Israel the flock was counted as it passed “under the rod” (Leviticus 27:32), and God told His people, “I will make you pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant” (Ezekiel 20:37). The rod meant each sheep was known and claimed. Hebrews applies the same truth to discipline: “For whom the LORD loves He chastens” (Hebrews 12:6).
hearing.hear: When the Lord corrects me, I don’t have to hear rejection. His discipline is a sign that I am His. A shepherd does not bother to correct a sheep that is not his own. Passing under His rod humbles me, and it also tells me I am counted, known, and claimed. I can receive His correction as comfort, because it means He will not let me be lost.

reflections.title: The Valley Is on the Path of Righteousness
reflections.html: Verse 4 follows straight after “He leads me in the paths of righteousness.” The dark valley is not a wrong turn. It is part of the right path. That answers a painful question many believers ask: “If I were really in God’s will, would I be in this darkness?” The Shepherd’s right paths sometimes go through dark valleys. Jesus was “led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” (Matthew 4:1). Paul went to Jerusalem “bound in the spirit,” knowing that “chains and tribulations” awaited him (Acts 20:22–23). Neither of them had missed God. Darkness is not proof that I have left the path. It may be proof that the path is going somewhere I could not reach any other way. Have I let a hard season convince me that I am out of God’s will?
reflections.q: Have I let a hard season convince me that I am out of God’s will?

reflections.title: Walked Through, Not Lived In
reflections.html: David says, “I walk through the valley.” He does not run in panic, and he does not set up camp. He walks, and he walks through. The valley is a passage, not a home. God promised, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow you” (Isaiah 43:2). Death is the last valley, but it is not the only one. Failure, illness, loneliness, depression, and grief are valleys too, and most of us walk through several in a lifetime. Each one feels permanent while we are in it. But the psalm keeps moving, from the valley to the table and on to the house. The valley is real, and it is temporary. What valley am I treating as a permanent address?
reflections.q: What valley am I treating as a permanent address?

reflections.title: The Valley of Deep Darkness
reflections.html: “The shadow of death” translates one Hebrew word, tsalmavet. It has traditionally been read as “shadow of death,” and many scholars read it as “deep darkness.” Either way, it names the darkest place a person can walk, whether death itself or any experience that feels like death. Isaiah used the word in a promise: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in the land of the shadow of death, upon them a light has shined” (Isaiah 9:2). Matthew says that promise was fulfilled when Jesus began His ministry in Galilee (Matthew 4:16). The darkest valley in the Old Testament became the place where the Light dawned. No darkness is so deep that the Shepherd will not walk through it with His sheep, and no darkness is so deep that His light cannot reach it.
reflections.q: “The shadow of death” translates one Hebrew word, tsalmavet .

reflections.title: A Shadow Cannot Bite
reflections.html: Spurgeon pointed out, “Nobody is afraid of a shadow, for a shadow cannot stop a man’s pathway even for a moment. The shadow of a dog cannot bite; the shadow of a sword cannot kill.” A shadow also means there is light somewhere beyond it. For the believer, death has become a shadow because Christ has removed its substance. He “abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10). Paul could taunt death: “O Death, where is your sting? O Hades, where is your victory?” (1 Corinthians 15:55). Death is still real, and we still grieve. But for those who belong to Christ, it has lost its power to destroy. The valley of the shadow of death leads to the house of the LORD. Do I fear death as a master, or face it as a shadow?
reflections.q: Do I fear death as a master, or face it as a shadow?

5.brief: The picture changes from shepherd to host: the LORD prepares a table for David in full view of his enemies, honors him as a welcomed guest by anointing his head with oil, and fills his cup to overflowing. Spiritually, the table points to communion with God amid the enemies that surround the soul, seen most fully at the Lord’s table (1 Corinthians 10:16), and the oil points to the Holy Spirit poured out on the believer.
5.explain:
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies;”

The picture changes from shepherd to host. The LORD is the same, and David is still speaking to Him directly. To “prepare a table” is to set out a meal, arranging the food for a guest. In David’s world a host who welcomed a guest to his table took responsibility for that guest’s protection and honor. David knew both sides of such a table. In the wilderness during Absalom’s revolt, friends brought food “for David and the people who were with him to eat” (2 Samuel 17:29), and as king he told Jonathan’s son, “you shall eat bread at my table continually” (2 Samuel 9:7).

The words “in the presence of my enemies” keep the danger in view. The enemies have not vanished. Yet the LORD’s welcome stands in full view of them, and the meal publicly honors and vindicates His guest. Long before, Israel had challenged God in the wilderness, “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Psalm 78:19). David answers with confident trust: the LORD does prepare a table, even with enemies looking on.

Read through the rest of Scripture, the table points to communion with God in the presence of the enemies that surround the soul: sin, the flesh, and the spiritual powers of darkness (Ephesians 6:12). The New Testament’s fullest picture of that communion is the Lord’s table: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16). Psalm 23 does not predict the Lord’s Supper, and the table does not make believers immune to temptation or opposition. But the enemies of the soul cannot cancel the welcome the Shepherd gives His own.

“You anoint my head with oil;”

Oil on the head was the honor and refreshment a host gave a welcomed guest. Jesus once said to a host who had neglected that courtesy, “You did not anoint My head with oil” (Luke 7:46). The verb here is not the word used for anointing kings and priests. It describes enriching and refreshing, so in David’s picture this is the honor of a guest, not a coronation.

Read through the rest of Scripture, oil points to the Holy Spirit. When Samuel anointed David, “the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward” (1 Samuel 16:13), and John tells believers that “the anointing which you have received from Him abides in you” (1 John 2:27). The Spirit refreshes and honors those who sit at the Shepherd’s table.

“My cup runs over.”

The host keeps his guest’s cup filled, and David’s cup overflows. The provision is more than enough. The psalm that began with “I shall not want” now pictures abundance beyond need, poured out by the same LORD.
5.notes:
“Prepare” translates ‘arak, to arrange or set in order, the same verb used for drawing up troops in battle order (1 Samuel 4:2). Psalm 78:19, quoted in the Verse Explanation, uses the same verb with the same noun for “table.”

“My enemies” translates a participle meaning those who show hostility, “my adversaries,” as Young’s Literal Translation renders it.

“Anoint” translates dashen, literally to make fat; the KJV margin reads “makest fat.” The verb for royal anointing is mashach, used when Samuel anointed David (1 Samuel 16:13).

“Runs over” translates a noun meaning saturation or abundance, revayah, so the Hebrew reads literally “my cup is abundance.” The only other occurrence of the noun is Psalm 66:12, “You brought us out to rich fulfillment.”

Some interpreters hold that the shepherd picture continues through verse 5. The table, the oil on the head, and the filled cup all belong to a meal given for a guest, which favors reading verse 5 as a change to the image of a host.

The NLT reads “You prepare a feast for me in the presence of my enemies. You honor me by anointing my head with oil. My cup overflows with blessings.”

hearing.observe: “You prepare a table” echoes one of Israel’s complaints in the desert. Psalm 78 remembers it: “Yes, they spoke against God: They said, ‘Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?’” (Psalm 78:19). David uses the same words and gives the answer: yes, He can, and He has. Israel and David both faced hard places with real needs. Unbelief stares at the desert and asks, “Can He?” Faith sits at the table and says, “You prepare a table before me.” And the table is strength for the road. The guest rises from it ready to go on.
hearing.hear: The Lord can provide for me in the hardest place I am in right now. The question is not whether He is able, but whether I will trust Him or doubt Him here. I want to stop asking “Can God?” while I stare at the wilderness, and start thanking Him for the table He has already set.

hearing.observe: The enemies have not gone away. They are still there, watching, and they cannot stop the meal. God does not wait for every enemy to leave before He feeds and honors His own. The point is not gloating over the enemy. The point is that the host’s welcome cannot be taken away. On the night of the Last Supper, Jesus told His disciples, “In the world you will have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).
hearing.hear: I don’t have to wait for every battle to end or every problem to disappear before I can enjoy God’s provision and peace. He welcomes me now, in the presence of whatever presses against me, and no enemy can cancel His invitation. I can sit down and eat in peace, even while the struggle goes on.

hearing.observe: “My cup runs over.” The cup is not just full; it spills over. A host who kept filling a guest’s cup was showing a generous welcome, not handing out the bare minimum. Jesus said, “I have come that they may have life, and that they may have it more abundantly” (John 10:10). He also promised that whoever believes in Him, “out of his heart will flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38), and John explains that He was speaking of the Spirit (7:39). The overflow Scripture celebrates is first of all the life God gives.
hearing.hear: My overflowing cup is not mainly about money or possessions. It is the life God pours into me: forgiveness I could never earn, mercy that meets me every morning, living water that does not run dry. When I count what He has poured into my life, the right response is thanksgiving. And what overflows from my cup is meant to spill onto others.

reflections.title: The Fugitive Becomes the Honored Guest
reflections.html: David knew both sides of a table like this. When he fled Jerusalem during Absalom’s revolt, friends brought beds, food, and supplies “for David and the people who were with him to eat. For they said, ‘The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness’” (2 Samuel 17:29). David ate as a fugitive, provided for by others. Years earlier, as king, he had found Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s lame son, and told him, “you shall eat bread at my table continually” (2 Samuel 9:7). David had been both the hungry guest and the generous host. In Psalm 23 the LORD is the host, and David is the guest. God welcomes those who have been on the run and gives them a place at His table. Do I come to God like a fugitive hoping for scraps, or like a guest He has invited?
reflections.q: Do I come to God like a fugitive hoping for scraps, or like a guest He has invited?

reflections.title: Know Your Enemies
reflections.html: David’s enemies were real men with real weapons. For believers, Scripture also names enemies that are less visible and just as real. There is sin: “abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul” (1 Peter 2:11). There is the flesh: “the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). And there is the devil: “your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Paul reminds us that “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12). The people who oppose us are not our deepest enemies. God sets His table in the presence of all of these. They may watch, accuse, and tempt, but they cannot take away the welcome God has given. Do I know who my real enemies are, or am I fighting people instead?
reflections.q: Do I know who my real enemies are, or am I fighting people instead?

reflections.title: The Table and the Cup of the New Covenant
reflections.html: Christians cannot read “You prepare a table” and “my cup” without thinking of the Lord’s Table. On the night He was betrayed, Jesus took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is shed for you” (Luke 22:20). Then He added, “But behold, the hand of My betrayer is with Me on the table” (Luke 22:21). Jesus Himself ate at a table in the presence of an enemy. Paul writes, “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16). Psalm 23 does not predict the Lord’s Supper, and Communion is not a charm against trouble. But the psalm’s picture finds its fullest meaning there: the LORD sets a table for His people, in a world still full of enemies, and fills their cup with the blessing of the new covenant. When I come to Communion, do I come as an honored guest at His table?
reflections.q: When I come to Communion, do I come as an honored guest at His table?
