reflections.title: Oil for the Head: Honor, Protection, and the Spirit
reflections.html: “You anoint my head with oil.” The verb here is not the word used for anointing kings. It is a word for refreshing and honoring someone. In its most likely sense, the verse continues the picture of a host. A good host poured oil on a guest’s head, and Jesus noticed when that honor was withheld: “You did not anoint My head with oil” (Luke 7:46). Some readers, however, think David is still picturing a shepherd caring for a sheep. Modern shepherding writers such as Phillip Keller describe shepherds applying oil to sheep’s heads to soothe them and keep off flies. The verse itself does not say this, and it should be held as a possible illustration rather than a description of ancient practice. If David had the sheep in mind, the oil is a picture of the Shepherd guarding His sheep from what would torment them. Either way, the oil speaks of the LORD’s honor and refreshing care. Across Scripture, oil also points to the Holy Spirit. When Samuel anointed David, “the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward” (1 Samuel 16:13). Believers have received “the anointing… from Him” that “abides in you” (1 John 2:27), and they are “sealed for the day of redemption” by the Spirit (Ephesians 4:30). The psalm does not say the oil means the Spirit, and the Hebrew verb does not mean a protective anointing. But these passages show that the Spirit is the one who now refreshes God’s people, abides in them, and keeps them sealed until the day of redemption. Do I welcome the Spirit’s refreshing, or try to push through without it?
reflections.q: Do I welcome the Spirit’s refreshing, or try to push through without it?

reflections.title: The Two Cups
reflections.html: Psalm 23 speaks of a cup that overflows with blessing. Scripture also speaks of another cup. “In the hand of the LORD there is a cup” of judgment (Psalm 75:8). Isaiah describes Jerusalem as having “drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury” (Isaiah 51:17). In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “O My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:39). Then He drank it. Because He drank the cup of wrath, believers now drink “the cup of blessing” (1 Corinthians 10:16). My cup runs over with mercy because His cup was filled with judgment. Every time I notice how full my cup is, I can remember what drinking the cup of judgment cost Jesus.
reflections.q: Psalm 23 speaks of a cup that overflows with blessing.

reflections.title: The Host Who Serves
reflections.html: In verse 5 the LORD waits on His guest. He prepares the table, anoints the head, and fills the cup. The God of the universe serves. Jesus showed the same heart. At the Last Supper He said, “I am among you as the One who serves” (Luke 22:27), and He washed His disciples’ feet (John 13:4–5). He even promised that when the Master returns and finds His servants watching, “he will gird himself and have them sit down to eat, and will come and serve them” (Luke 12:37). The King of glory delights to serve the people He loves. That changes how I come to Him. I do not have to earn a place at His table. And it changes how I treat others, because the people of a serving God become a serving people. Whom can I serve at my table this week?
reflections.q: Whom can I serve at my table this week?

6.brief: Where enemies once pursued David, he is sure that the LORD’s goodness and His mercy, His steadfast love, will pursue him all the days of his life, and that he will dwell in the house of the LORD, living in God’s presence for the length of his days. Scripture carries this hope on to unending dwelling with God (Revelation 21:3), the home to which the Shepherd leads His flock.
6.explain:
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me”

“Surely” expresses certainty. “Goodness” is God’s kindness and generous favor. “Mercy” is His steadfast, faithful love, the loyal love He has promised to His people. These are two distinct gifts, and David names both.

The verb “follow” usually means to pursue or chase, often in hostile pursuit. It is the verb used when Saul “pursued David in the Wilderness of Maon” (1 Samuel 23:25), and when David called after Saul, “Whom do you pursue?” (1 Samuel 24:14). Looking back, David can say that while enemies were hunting him, the LORD’s goodness and steadfast love were pursuing him. Read through the rest of Scripture, this is the Shepherd who goes “after the one which is lost until he finds it” (Luke 15:4).

“All the days of my life;”

The pursuit covers every day, the days in green pastures and the days in the dark valley alike. No stretch of David’s life lies outside the reach of God’s goodness and mercy.

“And I will dwell in the house of the LORD”

“The house of the LORD” named the sanctuary even before the temple was built; it was the place where Hannah went up to worship at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:7). For David it meant the place of God’s presence, and his great desire was “That I may dwell in the house of the LORD All the days of my life” (Psalm 27:4). To dwell there is to live in fellowship with God, not to take up literal residence in the tabernacle or temple. The guest welcomed at the table becomes one who belongs in the household.

Read through the rest of Scripture, this hope reaches its fulfillment in unending life with God. Jesus told His disciples, “In My Father’s house are many mansions” (John 14:2), and John heard the final announcement, “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3). The Shepherd who leads His flock through this life leads it home.

“Forever.”

The Hebrew expression behind “Forever” means “for length of days,” and it parallels “All the days of my life.” In David’s words its first meaning is the whole span of his life lived in God’s presence. Because Scripture goes on to reveal unending dwelling with God, believers rightly hear the eternal hope in it, without claiming that the Hebrew phrase alone means eternity.
6.notes:
“Surely” translates ’ak, which can mean “surely” or “only.” Young’s Literal Translation renders it “Only.”

“Goodness” and “mercy” translate two different Hebrew words, tov and hesed. In Psalm 52:1 the NKJV’s “goodness” translates hesed, but here “goodness” is tov and “mercy” is hesed. Other translations render hesed in this verse as “love” (NIV) or “lovingkindness” (NASB).

Some translators take radaph here in the sense of simple accompaniment rather than pursuit. The NLT makes the pursuit explicit: “Surely your goodness and unfailing love will pursue me.”

“I will dwell” involves a textual question. The Hebrew consonants can be read two ways. The Masoretic vowels read “and I will return,” from shuv. The Septuagint reads “and my dwelling” (kai to katoikein me), and Symmachus has the same sense; the Vulgate reads “I will dwell.” The preposition “in” fits “dwell” more naturally than “return,” and Psalm 27:4 uses the dwelling verb in the same phrase, “dwell in the house of the LORD All the days of my life.” The NKJV, ESV, NIV, and NASB all read “dwell.”

The KJV margin gives the literal sense, “to length of days.” The NKJV translates the same expression “forever” in Psalm 93:5: “Holiness adorns Your house, O LORD, forever.”

hearing.observe: “Follow” means more than tagging along. The Hebrew word usually means “pursue,” the same word used when Saul hunted David: “he pursued David in the Wilderness of Maon” (1 Samuel 23:25). David’s life was full of pursuers: Saul, and later the men of his own son Absalom. Here he uses the hunter’s word for God’s goodness and mercy. Some read the word more simply as “accompany,” but in David’s life it carries weight. Behind every human pursuer, a faster Pursuer was coming.
hearing.hear: What is chasing me is not my past failures or the enemy. God’s goodness and mercy are chasing me, and they are faster. When I feel hunted by fear or by what I have done, I can remember that love is pursuing me. If God chased me in judgment, I would run. Because He chases me in mercy, I can stop running and let myself be caught.

hearing.observe: “All the days of my life” comes from a man who has just walked through the valley of the shadow of death and eaten in the presence of enemies. David does not say goodness and mercy will follow him on the good days. He says all of them. Lamentations, written from the ruins of Jerusalem, says the same: “Through the LORD’s mercies we are not consumed, because His compassions fail not. They are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23). The promise covers the hospital days, the days of grief and failure, and the ordinary Tuesday.
hearing.hear: There is no day in my life when God’s goodness and mercy stop following me. Not the hardest day behind me, and not the hardest one ahead. Today counts too. I can look back on my worst seasons and see that His mercy was there, and I can face tomorrow knowing it will be there again.

hearing.observe: The psalm’s journey ends at a home. Pasture, valley, and table all lead to “the house of the LORD.” This was David’s deepest desire: “One thing I have desired of the LORD, that will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD” (Psalm 27:4). In David’s day the house of the LORD was the place of God’s presence among His people. Jesus carries the hope further: “In My Father’s house are many mansions” (John 14:2). At the end of the Bible, “the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3).
hearing.hear: Every day of my life is heading home to God’s presence, and that is the best thing I could want. The valley I am in now is not my destination. I want what David wanted: to live near my Shepherd, to see His beauty, all my days and forever.

reflections.title: Goodness and Mercy Are Two Different Gifts
reflections.html: “Goodness” (the Hebrew word tov) is God’s generous kindness, the good things He gives. “Mercy” (hesed) is His steadfast, covenant love, the loyal love that will not let go. Goodness gives what we do not deserve; mercy keeps holding on when we fail. Notice where they are. The Shepherd goes ahead to lead the sheep to water (verse 2). Goodness and mercy come behind (verse 6). The sheep is surrounded. “You have hedged me behind and before, and laid Your hand upon me” (Psalm 139:5). “The LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard” (Isaiah 52:12). God supplies what I need and holds on to me when I stumble. Which of these two gifts do I need to notice today?
reflections.q: Which of these two gifts do I need to notice today?

reflections.title: “Surely” Can Also Mean “Only.”
reflections.html: The small Hebrew word translated “surely” (’ak) can also mean “only.” Some read the line, “Only goodness and mercy shall follow me.” Both readings strengthen the promise. Nothing but goodness and mercy will follow me, and certainly goodness and mercy will follow me. David speaks this way after walking through the valley and sitting at the table. He is not guessing about the future. He has seen God’s care, and his past experience grounds his future confidence. When I look back on what God has already done, I can face what is ahead with the same certainty.
reflections.q: The small Hebrew word translated “surely” ( ’ak ) can also mean “only.”

reflections.title: “Forever” Means “Length of Days.”
reflections.html: “Forever” in this verse is literally “for length of days.” The phrase parallels “all the days of my life” in the line before. In its natural sense, David is confessing that he will dwell in the LORD’s presence for the whole length of his days. The same language can describe a long life on earth: “With long life I will satisfy him” (Psalm 91:16). Elsewhere it reaches further: “He asked life from You, and You gave it to him—length of days forever and ever” (Psalm 21:4). The rest of Scripture makes that horizon clear. Jesus promised, “In My Father’s house are many mansions… I will come again and receive you to Myself; that where I am, there you may be also” (John 14:2–3). At the end of the Bible, “the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3). David’s lifelong desire to dwell with God opens onto a hope that has no end. The valley is something we pass through. The house is where we stay. Do I think of eternal life as something far away, or as the unbroken continuation of living with God now?
reflections.q: Do I think of eternal life as something far away, or as the unbroken continuation of living with God now?
